Chapter 7. The Dangers of Dogmatic Thinking.
You know, there’s a certain comfort in feeling sure of things. When life feels overwhelming or unpredictable, it’s tempting to hang on to beliefs and rules that seem to bring order. But here’s the catch—chasing that sense of certainty can come with a real price.
Dogmatic thinking—where we stick to a set of ideas, no matter what—can be just as limiting as any authority telling us what to do.
Imagine a college student who’s trying to fit in. She joins a campus group that seems to have all the answers about right and wrong. At first, she feels relieved—finally, she belongs somewhere. But after a while, things change. She notices questions aren’t welcome. Dissent is met with criticism. The group’s beliefs are treated as absolute truth, and she starts echoing slogans she barely understands, hiding her own doubts just to keep the peace.
But dogma isn’t just about religion or politics. It can sneak into our workplaces, our families—even our friendships. It’s that insistent voice saying, “This is just how it’s done,” or, “People like us don’t do things differently.” It pushes us to fit in, to go along, to accept things at face value instead of being curious.
Most of us don’t even realize how easily we slip into dogmatic thinking. It feels safe, familiar—maybe even admirable. But after a while, it starts to close us off. It narrows our minds, stifles creativity, and makes it harder to be tolerant. Suddenly, the world turns into “us” versus “them,” leaving little space for nuance or empathy.
Picture a manager who’s convinced his way is the only way. He won’t listen to new ideas, and soon his team grows frustrated. Innovation grinds to a halt, resentment builds up, but he just can’t see it—he’s sure he’s right.
That’s the real risk of dogma. It shuts down growth. It makes questions feel threatening, and differences seem dangerous. People become afraid to think for themselves, to challenge the way things have always been, or to dream up new possibilities.
So, how do you break out of this mindset? It takes humility, curiosity, and a real willingness to admit you might be wrong. It means putting more value on asking questions than having quick answers, choosing real conversations over heated debates, and staying open instead of clinging to certainty.
The truth is, most people never make this leap. They hold tight to their beliefs, even when those beliefs stop working for them. But for the few who do let go, the rewards are pretty amazing. They find a world that’s richer, more complex, and way more alive. And maybe most important of all, they realize that wisdom isn’t about always having the answer—it’s about being brave enough to keep asking the questions.
